Figure 4. Day 3, Test F1. Flame growth from ignition to self-extinction
Figure 4 shows a typical test of ignition and flame growth. Although extinction occurred
at 45 s with the flame still growing, the heat flux was nearly steady by 30 s. Therefore a
heat of gasification (L) could be estimated. This was done in a preliminary estimation by
using the center heat flux sensor as the net average heat flux. If the heating is just due to
diffusion, theory indicates that the average heat flux is double the center value. Hence
such an estimated heat of gasification could be low by 50 %. On the other hand, if the
sensor is degraded in its calibration and radiation is a significant component of the heat
flux, then the estimate will also be low. Hence, using the center heat flux sensor directly
gives a conservatively low estimate of the heat of gasification in the emulation of real
solids. This will be significant when the totality of results for the 25 mm flat burning
surface is display over its spectrum of conservatively low values for L.
Figures 5 and 6 illustrate results for atmospheric conditions of 26.5 % oxygen and 0.7 atm
(10.2 psia), and 34 % oxygen and 0.56 atm (8.2 psia), respectively. Both use 50 % mixtures
of nitrogen and ethylene giving a fuel mixture heat of combustion of 21.8 kJ/g. Both of
these tests reached steady conditions and were terminated by shutting off the fuel.

… for the International Space Station (ISS) Increments 59 and 60
ACME Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
BRE Burning Rate Emulator
BRE is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, which uses a
single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels in the ISS’
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The investigation will be carried out in two separate rounds,
where the first round began in Increment 58 and was completed in Increment 59, so there is
nothing to be reported for Increment 60. The second round of testing will be conducted in
Increments 61 and/or 62.
Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project
Scientist, who is the primary contact for BRE and ACME information.
Principal Investigator (PI): Prof. James G. Quintiere, University of Maryland, College Park, MD
Co-Investigator (Co-I): Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, U. of Maryland, College Park, MD
Co-Investigator (Co-I): Dr. John L. de Ris, FM Global (retired)
Collaborator: Prof. Alexander Yu. Snegirev, Peter the Great St. Petersburg
Polytechnic University, St. Petersburg, Russia
Project Scientist (PS): Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH
PS team member: Dr. Uday G. Hegde, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH
I. Introduction
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack
(CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity
Experiments (ACME) project. BRE is focused on spacecraft fire prevention. More specifically,
BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as
extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the
relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments. A flat
porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where
measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the
vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent. A small number of gaseous fuels (including
mixtures with inert gases) are used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and
60

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
alcohol by matching properties including the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface
temperature, and smoke point. The experiment’s results can establish fuel properties that
directly relate to fire hazards in spacecraft, and if effective in microgravity could provide an
efficient, safe, and comprehensive technique for assessing flammability and selecting fire-
resistant spacecraft materials.
BRE’s specific experimental objectives are as follows, where it must be emphasized that NASA
does not currently plan to carry out the desired tests for objective B.
D. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2
mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients
with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA-considered
atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen; 10.2
psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to
a diverse range of condensed fuels.
E. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
F. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.
The observations will enable quantification of the microgravity behavior of condensed fuels (i.e.,
liquids and non-charring plastics).
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages
over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e.,
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Length
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot
free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity
testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the
gravitational environment of the combustion application.
II. Methods/Research Operations
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol
BRE and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.
The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most
common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and
the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.
61

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the operations center at the
NASA Glenn Research Center. The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in
a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry
stream. For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted after quasi-steady data has been
collected. But testing has not been conducted in a ‘manual’ mode thus far for BRE or
ACME in general.
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.
III. Results
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight
The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, where a total of 45 flames were
ignited during Increment 58. That round was completed in April 2019, during the
beginning of Increment 59, when an additional 17 flames were ignited. As such, a total
of 62 flames were ignited in the first round of testing. Meanwhile, the second round of
BRE testing is expected to begin near the end of Increment 61 and continue into
Increment 62. The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in
advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that
knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome.
All of the first round of tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while
burning ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen. The tests were carried out
at a range of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of
possible crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats. More specifically, testing
was especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2)
10.2 psia, 26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen. In all cases, the atmosphere was
diluted with nitrogen and any incomplete combustion products (e.g., water vapor and
carbon dioxide) from preceding tests. An exception is tests conducted after the chamber
atmosphere was vented and refilled, such as the first test of the day. But the atmosphere
was typically refreshed once during each of testing.
BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests are
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both
are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane (CH4)
is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the
absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting
62

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
because of its carbon double bond. Tests are conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed
with nitrogen, where the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch
for some cases. But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and
nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of
fuel concentrations.
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for BRE, where all of the ISS results are
electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently
planned ACME experiments.
A summary log of the flames ignited for BRE during the first round of testing - in
Increments 58 and 59 - is found in Table 1. The table includes a limited overview of the
test conditions. For completeness, a row was included for testing on April 1 (GMT 091)
even though it was quickly discovered that the hot-wire igniter tip had failed at the end
of the preceding test day. As a result, flames were not ignited until a few days later after
astronaut Nick Hague had replaced the igniter tip.

B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies
1. Mission anomalies
There were no significant anomalies hindering BRE operations during Increment 59,
but there was one in Increment 58 during the preparations for BRE testing began (that
was mistakenly not addressed in the 30-day report including that increment). It was
discovered on Feb. 4 (GMT 035) that the pressure was low in a check gas bottle for
the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). The bottle had been
on the space station for 9 years, and the low pressure was attributed to a nominal
leak rate. The check gas was for calibration of the GCIP measurements and not
needed for regular operations which proceeded unhindered. The bottle was replaced
on June 13 to enable the necessary calibration.
2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data
BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often
saturated. Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment
success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own
radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors. Estimates had been made of
the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the
flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the
radiometers. As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity. The
estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been
sufficiently tracked in the hardware development. Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted
as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the envisioned BRE test duration and 60
times the duration of the drop tests. With the fixed amplification of the radiometer
signals, the data was frequently lost - other than the knowledge that the limits were
exceeded. An engineering review failed to identify an acceptable solution and BRE
testing continued unchanged.
From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere:
The radiometry array proved problematic as its sensors were mostly out of range
and quickly became saturated. However, for some of the small size flames, these
data were complete. Those data will be vital to assessing the role of flame and
combustion product radiation.
Ignition was not always successful. As previously discussed, it was discovered on
April 1 (GMT 091) that the hot-wire igniter tip had failed on the preceding test day,
preventing further flame testing until it could be replaced. While such circumstances
are uncommon for ACME operations, BRE tests were sometimes conducted under
conditions, e.g., for igniter activation and deactivation, which led to momentary
flashes without sustained ignition. Given that unplanned crew time is required to
replace failed igniter tips, the BRE ops team limited - to varying degrees - the igniter
voltage and the time that it was energized within the flame. The latter was known
from earlier research in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) to degrade the hot-wire
64

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
igniter tip and hasten its demise. It is notable that the flashes of flame (across the
burner surface) sometimes continued briefly after the igniter was deactivated and
retracted. In one case on the first day of testing, there was excess fuel and a ‘fireball’
was ignited which promptly quenched. Ignition also sometimes failed due to a
software limitation where the fuelFlowIgnitionDeltaMs parameter which specifies the
relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation must be evenly divisible by 100
(ms). This limitation wasn’t initially understood and the igniter didn’t energize as a
result.
From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere:
It was realized that the igniter for the burner gases could only be applied for up to
4 seconds, on insertion and retraction. This produced an unanticipated problem,
as the time for the burner gases to reach the igniter could be tens of seconds
depending on the flow rate. Also, after the first test, the burner would contain
that fuel mixture mixed with the chamber gas. Thus the burner would need to be
flushed with nitrogen before the second fuel mixture was initiated.
Intense communication with the NASA team proceeded the day before the first
test. The gas volume of the burner along with the feed pipe volume was supplied
by NASA. Accordingly ground experiments at UMD were conducted with an
identical NASA BRE burner along with its piping volume from the flow valve.
These experiments and theory were used to develop an algorithm for determining
the relative timing of the igniter and gas flow activation that will result in ignition.
Day 1 was conducted with rough estimates made on the fly, and fortunately nearly
all of the tests led to a satisfactory ignition. By Day 2 an algorithm was established
and successfully used for the remainder of the testing. This algorithm will need to
be refined and applied for the larger 50 mm diameter burner that will be used in
Round 2.
A document on the development of the algorithm and its refinement for the larger burner
is being prepared and will be shared with the NASA team to facilitate round 2.
The second day of flame testing was delayed to allow for the development of a new
ignition procedure, where concerns arose that the mixture of gas flowing from the
burner wasn’t sufficiently well understood, i.e., in terms of concentrations. This
concern had to do with the burner’s large internal volume relative to that of the
burners used for the other ACME experiments. To be clear, this issue had to do with
the analysis of results rather than the achievement of ignition. Re-planning was also
necessary early in BRE testing because the test durations were often much longer than
had earlier been envisioned by the investigators. While these factors didn’t directly
interfere with the acquisition of test data, they did slow progress.

While it rarely occurred, BRE tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the
controlling software script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation
of the igniter. As a result, there is little lost other than the time associated with the
failed test attempt. Such aborts typically occur because of communication issues with
an Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU).
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel and nitrogen
have unfortunately not always performed adequately, where the flow rates have not
always been appropriately steady. The resulting effects on the flame behavior are
tentatively assumed to be minor, but this still needs to be assessed.
C. Completeness/Quality of Data
The number of flames ignited in Increments 58 and 59 significantly exceeds the planned
tests – under the tested conditions (25 mm burner and ethylene as fuel) - which were
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD). A
total of 25 such tests were required, while 62 flames with those conditions were ignited.
As such, more than twice as many flames were ignited as had been planned.
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not necessarily available for
all tests. Recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is done
because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed
per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some
image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted. This
is intentionally done to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the
project constraints.
From BRE Co-I Peter Sunderland:
The video and image data of the testing produced satisfactory data to display the
nature of the burning sequence from ignition to self-extinction or fuel termination.
However, the image quality is less than was hoped for. The ACME ops camera provides
video, but only offers 0.3 megapixels of resolution, and for many flames it is too
zoomed out. The GigE camera has poor sensitivity in the blue, and after the ignition
transient all our flames have been blue. This camera only offers 1.4 megapixels of
resolution and requires about 1 s exposures for blue flames, which is far too slow to
be considered video. The images provided by both cameras are, according to UMD
marketing staff, at too low resolution to be used in press releases. In round 2 we will
increase the gain on the GigE camera, an option we were unaware of in round 1.
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware. But neglecting that
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually
become ‘hot’ over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing,
they are a degradation of the image quality.
66

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
See discussion in III.D in regard to fouling or degradation of the paint on the BRE burner’s
heat flux sensors.
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS). In this regard,
note that the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS).
Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has
been secured and BRE’s first round, completed in Increment 59, is considered to be
successful despite the frequent saturation of the radiometer data discussed in section
III.B.2.
D. Status of Data Analysis (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral student
Parham Dehghani)
All measured transient raw data (e.g., heat flux sensors, thermocouples, radiometers,
mass flow meters and chamber pressure sensor) have been converted to engineering
units and plotted using the calibrations provided in ACME’s Software Interface Design
Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D).
All of the round 1 tests have had the heat flux sensor data reduced using their original
calibrations. As presented below, the data is being processed to address the effect of the
combustion product water and paint degradation.
The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from
the flame to the burner surface. In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass
flow rate per unit area of the fuel mixture gives the heat of gasification of the emulated
fuel. The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of
gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in
an inert matrix). Thus, achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real
solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than for a candle flame, this
has not been shown before.
The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface.
One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center. The resulting data suffered
from two possible effects. The first effect is the condensation of water vapor. As the
sensors are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the flame grows, water from its
combustion products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor. This occurs, as
the dew point for combustion products is about 60-70oC, and the sensor begins at
ambient temperature and can achieve temperatures over 100oC. Thus, condensation can
occur at temperatures below the dew point that leads to added heat to the sensor. Above
the dew point, the condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor.
67

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
When the sensor is dry and above 100oC, it will only measure the heat flux from the flame
gases as intended.
We have duplicated this condensation effect in 1-g laboratory experiments with our
duplicative NASA BRE burner. Fig. 1 illustrates the condensation and evaporation effect
in the ISS tests. The offset sensor in red shows a clear jump increase when the water
fully evaporates. More analysis is needed to properly correct for this effect. Fortunately,
by the end of the test shown here (and for all of the other data), this water effect is gone.
Figure 1. Typical net heat flux of the heat flux sensors.
The second effect on the heat flux sensors is that the heat may have fouled their paint.
This could then affect their calibration. Figure 2 shows an image of the ISS burner after
round 1 tests were concluded. It can be seen that the paint on the sensors is degraded.
This was the original manufacturer’s paint, instead of that used for the copper top. The
copper paint appears fine. We are working with the heat flux gage manufacturer to
explore the effect of heat damage on the calibration of the sensors. This will give us a
way to determine a quantitative change in the calibration.

Preliminary analysis of the radiometer sensor data has indicated its consistent ability to
measure the flame overall radiation heat loss fraction. The method to determine the
radiative heat flux component to the burner is more complex, and it will rely on
theoretical modeling. This will take some time.
The video images of all the flames have been compiled and are being quantified in terms
of flame shapes.
Alexander Snegirev, our Russian partner, has attempted a numerical simulation of at least
one of the ISS BRE tests. That work is still in progress. It should be remarked his student
won the Student Prize for Best Presentation at the 9th International Seminar on Fire and
Explosion Hazards held in St. Petersburg, Russia in April 2019 for simulating our 5-s BRE
drop tests.
E. Preliminary Research Findings (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral
student Parham Dehghani)
Despite having much data to digest and analyze, there is a profound conclusion from
these tests. The burner has definitively shown that steady burning is possible for real
solids with a flat surface of 25 mm diameter. Up to now most flammability studies in
microgravity have focused on flame spread with a wind for concurrent spread and at least
a self-induced wind for opposed flow spread. We already knew that this would be
possible from normal-gravity research. The burning of liquids, as in a wick of a candle
flame and small droplets, has been shown to produce steady flames. However, many
droplet flames were found to extinguish owing to radiative cooling of the flame. We see
this as well in the extended ISS microgravity tests. However, this extinction was
predominately seen for atmospheric conditions of 21% oxygen and 14.7 psia. At
conditions of 27% oxygen, 10.2 psia and 34% oxygen, 8.2 psia, the flames generally
persisted for 2 minutes or more. These are all atmospheric conditions that NASA is
considering for future spacecraft. Some examples are shown below to illustrate these
results.
Figure 5 shows a typical test of ignition and flame growth. Although extinction occurred
at 45 s with the flame still growing, the heat flux was nearly steady by 30 s. Therefore, a
heat of gasification (L) could be estimated. This was done in a preliminary estimation by
using the center heat flux sensor as the net average heat flux. If the heating is just due to
diffusion, theory indicates that the average heat flux is double the center value. Hence
such an estimated heat of gasification could be low by 50%. On the other hand, if the
sensor is degraded in its calibration and radiation is a significant component of the heat
flux, then the estimate will also be low. Hence, using the center heat flux sensor directly
gives a conservatively low estimate of the heat of gasification in the emulation of real
solids. This will be significant when the totality of results for the 25 mm flat burning
surface is displayed over its spectrum of conservatively low values for L.

30-day Operational Accomplishments Report
… for the International Space Station (ISS) Increment 63
ACME Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
BRE Burning Rate Emulator
BRE is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, which uses a
single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels in the ISS’
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The investigation is being carried out in two separate rounds,
where the first round was conducted during Increments 58 and 59 and the second round began
in Increment 63 and should be completed in Increment 64.
Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project
Scientist, who is the primary contact for BRE and ACME information.
Principal Investigator (PI): Prof. James G. Quintiere, University of Maryland, College Park, MD
Co-Investigator (Co-I): Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, U. of Maryland, College Park, MD
Co-Investigator (Co-I): Dr. John L. de Ris, FM Global (retired)
Collaborator: Prof. Alexander Yu. Snegirev, Peter the Great St. Petersburg
Polytechnic University, St. Petersburg, Russia
Project Scientist (PS): Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH
PS team member: Dr. Uday G. Hegde, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH
I. Introduction
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack
(CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity
Experiments (ACME) project. BRE is focused on spacecraft fire prevention. More specifically,
BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as
extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the
relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments. A flat
porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where
measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the
vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent. A small number of gaseous fuels (including
mixtures with inert gases) are used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and
alcohol by matching properties including the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface
79

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
temperature, and smoke point. The experiment’s results can establish fuel properties that
directly relate to fire hazards in spacecraft, and if effective in microgravity could provide an
efficient, safe, and comprehensive technique for assessing flammability and selecting fire-
resistant spacecraft materials.
BRE’s specific experimental objectives are as follows, where it must be emphasized that NASA
does not currently plan to carry out the desired tests for objective B.
G. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2
mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients
with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA-considered
atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen; 10.2
psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to
a diverse range of condensed fuels.
H. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
I. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.
The observations will enable quantification of the microgravity behavior of condensed fuels (i.e.,
liquids and non-charring plastics).
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages
over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e.,
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Length
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot
free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity
testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the
gravitational environment of the combustion application.
II. Methods/Research Operations
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol
BRE and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.
The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most
common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and
the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the operations center at the
NASA Glenn Research Center. The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in
80

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it could
alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control
parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in
the telemetry stream. For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted after quasi-steady
data has been collected. But testing has not been conducted in a ‘manual’ mode thus far
for BRE or ACME in general.
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.
III. Results
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight
The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, during Increment 58, when a total of
45 flames were ignited. That round was completed in April 2019, during Increment 59,
when an additional 17 flames were ignited. As such, a total of 62 flames were ignited in
the first round of testing. Meanwhile, the BRE’s second-round flame testing began in
Sept. 2020, during Increment 63, during which 47 flames were ignited. The second and
final round of tests should be completed during Increment 64.
The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable
the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second
round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. However, the break was longer than
had been planned because of combination of hardware issues and limited crew
availability. As a result, BRE’s second round was rescheduled to occur after both rounds
of the preceding ACME experiment, Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames
(s-Flame), was completed, where that occurred in July 2020. A factor in that decision was
the delayed start of commercial crew launches and understanding that crew availability
would be limited until such crew launches entered an operational, rather than
demonstration, phase.
All first-round tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning
ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen. The tests were carried out at a range
of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible
crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats. More specifically, testing was
especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia,
26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen. In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with
nitrogen and any incomplete combustion products (e.g., water vapor and carbon dioxide)
from preceding tests. An exception is tests conducted after the chamber atmosphere was
81

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
vented and refilled, such as the first test of the day. But during tests days, the atmosphere
was typically refreshed once or twice between sets of tests.
Second round testing is being carried out including both BRE burner diameters, i.e., 25
and 50 mm, and on some days with methane (CH4) – again sometimes diluted with
nitrogen. Therefore, the second round of tests features a broader range of conditions
than investigated during the first round.
BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests are
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both
are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane (CH4)
is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the
absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting
because of its carbon double bond. Tests are conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed
with nitrogen, where the fuel and nitrogen were premixed on the ground prior to launch
for some cases. But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and
nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of
fuel concentrations.
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for BRE, where all ISS results are
electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently
planned ACME experiments.

B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies
1. Mission anomalies
There were no significant anomalies hindering BRE operations during Increments 59
and 63, but there was one in Increment 58 during the preparations for BRE testing
(that was mistakenly not addressed in the 30-day report including that increment). It
was discovered on Feb. 4 (GMT 035) that the pressure was low in a check gas bottle
for the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP). The bottle had
been on the space station for 9 years, and the low pressure was attributed to a
nominal leak rate. The check gas was for calibration of the GCIP measurements and
not needed for regular operations which proceeded unhindered. The bottle was
replaced on June 13 to enable the necessary calibration.

2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data
BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often
saturated. Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment
success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own
radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors. Estimates had been made of
the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the
flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the
radiometers. As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity. The
estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been
sufficiently tracked in the hardware development. Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted
as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the envisioned BRE test duration and 60
times the duration of the drop tests. With the fixed amplification of the radiometer
signals, the data was frequently lost - other than the knowledge that the limits were
exceeded. An engineering review failed to identify an acceptable solution and BRE
testing continued unchanged.
From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere:
The radiometry array proved problematic as its sensors were mostly out of range
and quickly became saturated. However, for some of the small size flames, these
data were complete. Those data will be vital to assessing the role of flame and
combustion product radiation.
Ignition was not always successful. As previously discussed, it was discovered on 1
April 2019 (GMT 091) that the hot-wire igniter tip had failed on the preceding test
day, preventing further flame testing until it could be replaced. While such
circumstances are uncommon for ACME operations, BRE tests were sometimes
conducted under conditions, e.g., for igniter activation and deactivation, which led to
momentary flashes without sustained ignition. Given that unplanned crew time is
required to replace failed igniter tips, the BRE ops team limited - to varying degrees -
the igniter voltage and the time that it was energized within the flame. The latter was
known from earlier research in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) to degrade the
hot-wire igniter tip and hasten its demise. It is notable that the flashes of flame
(across the burner surface) sometimes continued briefly after the igniter was
deactivated and retracted. In one case on the first day of testing, there was excess
fuel and a ‘fireball’ was ignited which promptly quenched. Ignition also sometimes
failed due to a software limitation where the fuelFlowIgnitionDeltaMs parameter
which specifies the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation must be
evenly divisible by 100 (ms). This limitation wasn’t initially understood and the igniter
didn’t energize as a result.
84

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere:
It was realized that the igniter for the burner gases could only be applied for up to
4 seconds, on insertion and retraction. This produced an unanticipated problem,
as the time for the burner gases to reach the igniter could be tens of seconds
depending on the flow rate. Also, after the first test, the burner would contain
that fuel mixture mixed with the chamber gas. Thus the burner would need to be
flushed with nitrogen before the second fuel mixture was initiated.
Intense communication with the NASA team proceeded the day before the first
test. The gas volume of the burner along with the feed pipe volume was supplied
by NASA. Accordingly ground experiments at UMD were conducted with an
identical NASA BRE burner along with its piping volume from the flow valve.
These experiments and theory were used to develop an algorithm for determining
the relative timing of the igniter and gas flow activation that will result in ignition.
Day 1 [of the first round] was conducted with rough estimates made on the fly,
and fortunately nearly all of the tests led to a satisfactory ignition. By Day 2 an
algorithm was established and successfully used for the remainder of the testing.
This algorithm will need to be refined and applied for the larger 50 mm diameter
burner that will be used in Round 2.
A document on the development of the algorithm and its refinement for the larger
burner [was] prepared and … shared with the NASA team to facilitate [ignition in]
round 2.
The second day of round-1 flame testing was delayed to allow for the development of
a new ignition procedure, where concerns arose that the mixture of gas flowing from
the burner wasn’t sufficiently well understood, i.e., in terms of concentrations. This
concern had to do with the burner’s large internal volume relative to that of the
burners used for the other ACME experiments. To be clear, this issue had to do with
the analysis of results rather than the achievement of ignition. Re-planning was also
necessary early in BRE testing because the test durations were often much longer than
had earlier been envisioned by the investigators. While these factors didn’t directly
interfere with the acquisition of test data, they did slow progress.
While it rarely occurred, BRE tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the
controlling software script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation
of the igniter. As a result, there is little lost other than the time associated with the
failed test attempt. Such aborts typically occur because of communication issues with
an Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU).
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel and nitrogen
have unfortunately not always performed adequately, where the flow rates have not

always been appropriately steady. The resulting effects on the flame behavior are
tentatively assumed to be minor, but this still needs to be assessed.
While it didn’t prevent the acquisition of scientific data, the intended igniter arm,
which establishes the relative positioning of the igniter tip and burner, was not found
for the round-2 hardware set-up. Therefore, an alternate arm, which positioned the
igniter further from the burner than intended, was used for the 3 Sept. 2020 testing.
Fortunately, the flames were still reliably ignited and the proper igniter arm was found
and installed prior to the subsequent test day.
However, it was determined that the 3 Sept. 2020 science objectives were not
accomplished because the fuel didn’t always transition to the intended test flow rate.
As a result of concerns about the ignition success because of the use of the alternate
igniter arm, the decision was made to repeatedly ignite the flame at the same fuel
flow rate and then subsequently adjust it to the desired test flow rate. The first
attempt was successful, but the transition time was shortened to save fuel, etc. which
unfortunately prevented the flow transition. In other words, the transition time was
too short where that wasn’t discovered until review of the data days later. As a result,
the tests were generally conducted at the same fuel flow rate, where that was meant
to be a variable. As a result, the data currently doesn’t allow a full assessment of the
effect of the burner size on the flammability. Therefore, a make-up test day in
Increment 64 has been planned to address this shortcoming.
C. Completeness/Quality of Data
The number of flames ignited in Increments 58 and 59 significantly exceeds the planned
tests – under the tested conditions (25 mm burner and ethylene as fuel) - which were
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD). A
total of 25 such tests were required, while 62 flames with those conditions were ignited.
As such, more than twice as many flames were ignited as had been planned.
An additional 48 tests were specified as required in the ISRD to fully accomplish the BRE
science objectives, i.e., where a total of 73 test points were required. While there were
issues with the Increment 63 testing, e.g., discussed in section B, 47 flames were ignited
in Sept.-Oct. 2020, where 6 additional test days are currently planned for Increment 64
(including the make-up day previously discussed). As such, it is expected that far more
tests will be conducted than had been originally planned for BRE’s second round.
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not necessarily available for
all tests. Recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is done
because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed
per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some
image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted. This
is intentionally done to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the
project constraints.
86

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
From BRE Co-I Peter Sunderland:
The video and image data of the testing produced satisfactory data to display the
nature of the burning sequence from ignition to self-extinction or fuel termination.
However, the image quality is less than was hoped for. The ACME ops camera
provides video, but only offers 0.3 megapixels of resolution, and for many flames it is
too zoomed out. The GigE camera has poor sensitivity in the blue, and after the
ignition transient all our flames have been blue. This camera only offers 1.4
megapixels of resolution and requires about 1 s exposures for blue flames, which is
far too slow to be considered video. The images provided by both cameras are,
according to UMD marketing staff, at too low resolution to be used in press releases.
In round 2 we will increase the gain on the GigE camera, an option we were unaware
of in round 1.
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware. But neglecting that
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually
become ‘hot’ over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing,
they are a degradation of the image quality.
See the discussion in III.D regarding fouling or degradation of the paint on the BRE
burner’s heat flux sensors.
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there
is not obvious indication of this and it has thus far not been evaluated with available
measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS). Note that
although the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is conducted, is
equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS) it was not utilized for BRE (or any
ACME) testing because of the crew time needed to enable and disable the isolation before
and after testing.
Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has
been secured and BRE’s first round is considered to be successful despite the frequent
saturation of the radiometer data discussed in section III.B.2.
D. Status of Data Analysis (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral student
Parham Dehghani)
All measured transient raw data (e.g., heat flux sensors, thermocouples, radiometers,
mass flow meters and chamber pressure sensor) have been converted to engineering
units and plotted using the calibrations provided in ACME’s Software Interface Design
Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D).
All of the round 1 tests have had the heat flux sensor data reduced using their original
calibrations. As presented below, the data is being processed to address the effect of the
combustion product water condensation on the sensor surfaces.
87

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from
the flame to the burner surface. In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass
flow rate per unit area of the fuel mixture gives the heat of gasification of the emulated
fuel. The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of
gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in
an inert matrix). Thus, achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real
solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than for a candle flame, this
has not been shown before.
The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface.
One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center (r = 9.5 mm). As the sensors
are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the flame grows, water from its combustion
products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor. This occurs, as the dew point
for combustion products is about 60-70oC, and the sensor begins at ambient temperature
and can achieve temperatures over 100oC. Thus, condensation can occur at
temperatures below the dew point that leads to added heat to the sensor. Above the
dew point, the condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor. When
the sensor is dry and above 100oC, it will only measure the heat flux from the flame gases
as intended.
We have duplicated this condensation effect in 1-g laboratory experiments with the
duplicative NASA BRE burner. Fig. 1 illustrates the condensation and evaporation effect
in the ISS tests. The offset sensor in red shows a clear jump increase when the water fully
evaporates. More analysis is needed to properly correct for this effect. Fortunately, by
the end of the test shown here (and for all of the other data), this water effect is gone.
Figure 1. Typical net heat flux of the heat flux sensors.
88

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
The second effect on the heat flux sensors is that the heat may have fouled their paint.
This could then affect their calibration. Figure 2 shows an image of the ISS burner after
round 1 tests were concluded. It can be seen that the paint on the sensors is degraded.
This was the original manufacturer’s paint, instead of that used for the copper top. The
copper paint appears fine. We worked with the heat flux gage manufacturer to explore
the effect of heat damage on the calibration of the sensors. The results showed that the
calibration was stable and didn’t change during the process of heating and cooling.
Figure 2. Paint degradation on heat flux sensors.
The second technique to determine the heat flux is the copper calorimeter forming the
top of the burner. The temperature rise of the copper is key to that determination.
Figure 3 shows that typically the copper temperature is nearly uniform and smooth in
time. It does not appear that condensation or evaporation is having any effect on its
temperature behavior. So, we believe we are justified in using this measurement to
predict the overall average heat flux from the flame to the burner.

Our analysis of the radiometer sensor data has indicated its consistent ability to measure
the flame overall radiation heat loss fraction. The method to determine the radiative heat
flux component to the burner is more complex, and it is based on the geometrical details
of the radiometers and burner surface relative distance and orientation. Also, the burner
surface will re-radiate heat that impinges the radiometer and it needs to be corrected. All
of the available radiation data are processed for the first round of testing and an empirical
radiation correlation with flame height is found.
The video images of all the flames have been compiled and are being quantified in terms
of flame shapes. Also, a summary booklet of all of the key findings along with heat flux
and surface temperature data for each test was compiled.
Alexander Snegirev, our Russian partner, has attempted a numerical simulation of at least
one of the ISS BRE tests. That work is still in progress. It should be remarked his student
won the Student Prize for Best Presentation at the 9th International Seminar on Fire and
Explosion Hazards held in St. Petersburg, Russia in April 2019 for simulating our 5-s BRE
drop tests.
E. Preliminary Research Findings (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral
student Parham Dehghani)
The burner has shown that quasi-steady burning is possible for real solids with a flat
surface of 25 mm diameter. Up to now most flammability studies in microgravity have
focused on flame spread with a wind for concurrent spread and at least a self-induced
wind for opposed flow spread. We already knew that this would be possible from normal-
gravity research. The burning of liquids, as in a wick of a candle flame and small droplets,
has been shown to produce steady flames. However, many droplet flames were found to
extinguish owing to radiative cooling of the flame. We see this as well in the extended
ISS microgravity tests. However, this extinction was predominately seen for nominal
ambient conditions of 21% oxygen and 14.7 psia. At conditions of 27% oxygen, 10.2 psia
and 34% oxygen, 8.2 psia, the flames generally persisted for 3 minutes or more. These are
all atmospheric conditions that NASA is considering for future spacecraft
Figure 5 shows a typical test of ignition and flame growth. Although extinction occurred
at 45 s with the flame still growing, the heat flux was nearly steady by 30 s. Therefore, a
heat of gasification (L) could be estimated. This was done by using the arithmetic average
of the center and offset heat flux sensor as the net average heat flux.

A simple analysis based on geometrical view factor of surface with respect to the flame
sheet, allowed us to estimate the fraction of the total available heat that impinges
surface. Also, the analytical model (the Ellipsoidal model) based on classical diffusion
theory was used to estimate the convective heat flux to the surface which are shown by
Figures 12 and 13, respectively. Adding up the convective, radiative and re-radiation from
surface results in total average heat flux that gives theoretical heats of gasification when
divided by fuel mixture mass flux.

However, both plots show the heat of gasification is up to 20 % higher for the lower heat

flux. But again, the data mostly cluster about one trend line except for very low heats of
combustion. However, the 1-g corresponding heat of combustion data shift far to the

Let us interpret Figures 14 and 15 in terms of the flammability of real materials in
microgravity. Typical melting plastics have heats of gasification ranging from about 2 to
3 kJ/g, with effective heats of gasification for charring plastics above 4 kJ/g. Some
selected literature values for materials with heats of combustion in the BRE range are
listed in Table 3. The accuracy of the calorimeter heat flux is found to be less than the
two sensors, thus, we relied on the arithmetic average of the two heat flux sensors data
for obtaining the flammability map. However, same results are shown considering the
calorimeter data. Figure 14. would suggest that polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP)
would burn in microgravity at about 3 g/m2s. Nylon and PMMA would burn at about 2.5
g/m2s, and the phenolic glass fiber composite would burn at about 1 g/m2s.

One important fire safety consideration, based on the findings of this study, is that solid
materials with heats of combustion in the range 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification
from about 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn in microgravity. The NASA alternative flammability Test
2 [1] using the Cone Calorimeter can measure these material properties. As this study
develops a more complete understanding, NASA may wish to put more emphasis into Test
2.
Moreover, the flammability map based on our theoretical analysis is shown in Figure 16.
It shows similar asymptotic trend and clearly indicates lower pressure and higher oxygen
concentration as favorable conditions for long duration burning.

The imaging data from ops camera and ACME camera are used to create videos and image
sequences for all of the tests taken so far. Preliminary analysis on the first three days of
the second round of ISS testing data are performed. Many of the first day tests with the
50-mm BRE burner were not at the intended flow rate. A make-up day will be carried out
to accomplish the day’s scientific objectives. The second day plan contained a
combination of pure and diluted ethylene at 3 different ambient conditions. Pure
methane was the fuel used for testing on the third day at 3 different nominal ambient
conditions. It was observed that methane was hard to ignite compared to ethylene and
flames tend to self-extinguish faster even at a high oxygen concentration.
A new method is used to observe the asymptotic behavior of the heat flux data. The

… for the International Space Station (ISS) Increment 64
ACME Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
BRE Burning Rate Emulator
BRE is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, which uses a
single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels in the ISS’
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The investigation was carried out in two separate rounds,
where the first and second rounds were respectively conducted during Increments 58-59 and 63-
64. While this report was prepared for Increment 64, it comprehensively addresses the operations
in all four increments.
Prepared by the PI team and Dennis Stocker (dennis.p.stocker@nasa.gov), the ACME Project
Scientist, who is the primary contact for BRE and ACME information.
Principal Investigator (PI): Prof. James G. Quintiere, University of Maryland, College Park, MD
Co-Investigator (Co-I): Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, U. of Maryland, College Park, MD
Co-Investigator (Co-I): Dr. John L. de Ris, FM Global (retired)
Collaborator: Prof. Alexander Yu. Snegirev, Peter the Great St. Petersburg
Polytechnic University, St. Petersburg, Russia
Project Scientist (PS): Dennis P. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH
PS team member: Dr. Uday G. Hegde, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH
I. Introduction
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack
(CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity
Experiments (ACME) project. BRE is focused on spacecraft fire prevention. More specifically,
BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as
extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the
relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments. A flat
porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where
measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the
vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent. A small number of gaseous fuels (including
mixtures with inert gases) are used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and
108

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
alcohol by matching properties including the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface
temperature, and smoke point. The experiment’s results can establish fuel properties that
directly relate to fire hazards in spacecraft, and if effective in microgravity could provide an
efficient, safe, and comprehensive technique for assessing flammability and selecting fire-
resistant spacecraft materials.
BRE’s specific experimental objectives are as follows, where it must be emphasized that NASA
does not currently plan to carry out the desired tests for objective B.
J. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2
mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2
ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA-
considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 %
oxygen; 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can
be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels.
K. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
L. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.
The observations will enable quantification of the microgravity behavior of condensed fuels (i.e.,
liquids and non-charring plastics).
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages
over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e.,
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Length
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot
free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity
testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the
gravitational environment of the combustion application.
II. Methods/Research Operations
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol
BRE and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.
The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most
common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and
the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.
109

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the operations center at the
NASA Glenn Research Center. The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in
a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it could
alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control
parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in
the telemetry stream. For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted after quasi-steady
data has been collected. But testing has not been conducted in a ‘manual’ mode thus far
for BRE or ACME in general.
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.
III. Results
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight
The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, during Increment 58, when a total of
45 flames were ignited. That round was completed in April 2019, during Increment 59,
when an additional 17 flames were ignited. BRE’s second-round flame testing began in
Sept. 2020, during Increment 63, in which 47 flames were ignited. The second and final
round of tests was completed in Jan. 2021, during Increment 64, when another 85 flames
were ignited. As a result, 62 and 132 flames were respectively ignited in the first and
second rounds of testing for a total of 194 flames.
The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable
the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second
round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. However, the break was longer than
had been planned because of combination of hardware issues and limited crew
availability. As a result, BRE’s second round was rescheduled to occur after both rounds
of the preceding ACME experiment, Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames
(s-Flame), was completed, where that occurred in July 2020. A factor in that decision was
the delayed start of commercial crew launches and understanding that crew availability
would be limited until such crew launches entered an operational, rather than
demonstration, phase.
All first-round tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning
ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen. The tests were carried out at a range
of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible
crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats. More specifically, testing was
especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia,
26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen. In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with
110

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
nitrogen and any combustion products (e.g., water vapor and carbon dioxide) from
preceding tests. An exception is tests conducted after the chamber atmosphere was
vented and refilled, such as the first test of the day. But during tests days, the atmosphere
was typically refreshed once or twice between sets of tests.
Second round testing was carried out including both BRE burner diameters, i.e., 25 and
50 mm, and on some days with methane (CH4) – again sometimes diluted with nitrogen.
Therefore, the second round of tests featured a broader range of conditions than
investigated during the first round. However, in contrast to the first round most of the
round 2 tests were carried out at roughly 14.7 psia, although pressure has a secondary
effect on flames. Meanwhile, the tests in this round were carried out at various oxygen
concentrations as in the first round but were more often conducted with ~40% oxygen,
where oxygen of course has a strong effect on combustion.
BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests are
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both
are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood. Methane (CH4)
is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the
absence of carbon-carbon bonds. Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting
because of its carbon double bond. Tests are conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed
with nitrogen, where the fuel and nitrogen were premixed on the ground prior to launch
for some cases. But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and
nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of
fuel concentrations.
There are no samples (e.g., of soot) collected for BRE, where all ISS results are
electronically transmitted to the ground. That is furthermore the case for all currently
planned ACME experiments.

of tests) and Increment 63 and 64 (the second round) is found in Table 1. The table
includes a limited overview of the test conditions. For completeness, a row was included

wire igniter tip had failed at the end of the preceding test day. As a result, flames were
not ignited until a few days later after astronaut Nick Hague had replaced the igniter tip.

been on the space station for 9 years, and the low pressure was attributed to a
nominal leak rate. The check gas was for calibration of the GCIP measurements and
not needed for regular operations which proceeded unhindered. The bottle was

The anomaly in Increment 64 was similar in that there was a slow leak of the GCIP’s
argon carrier gas. As a result, the bottle valves for all of the instrument’s gas bottles
were closed on Dec. 29, 2020 (GMT 364) making those measurements unavailable for
the BRE’s last three test days.
2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data
BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often
saturated. Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment
success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own
radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors. Estimates had been made of
the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the
flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the
radiometers. As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity. The
estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been
sufficiently tracked in the hardware development. Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted
as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the envisioned BRE test duration and 60
times the duration of the drop tests. With the fixed amplification of the radiometer
signals, the data was frequently lost - other than the knowledge that the limits were
exceeded. An engineering review failed to identify an acceptable solution and BRE
testing continued unchanged during the first round, i.e., during increments 58 and 59.
From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere:
The radiometry array proved problematic as its sensors were mostly out of range
and quickly became saturated. However, for some of the small size flames, these
data were complete. Those data will be vital to assessing the role of flame and
combustion product radiation.
Saturation of the radiometers was partially mitigated in the round 2 testing, during
increments 63 and 64, through use of ACME’s standard array instead of the one
developed specifically for BRE.
Ignition was not always successful. As previously discussed, it was discovered on 1
April 2019 (GMT 091) that the hot-wire igniter tip had failed on the preceding test
day, preventing further flame testing until it could be replaced. While such
circumstances are uncommon for ACME operations, BRE tests were sometimes
conducted under conditions, e.g., for igniter activation and deactivation, which led to
momentary flashes without sustained ignition. Given that unplanned crew time is
required to replace failed igniter tips, the BRE ops team limited - to varying degrees -
the igniter voltage and the time that it was energized within the flame. The latter was
113

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
known from earlier research in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) to degrade the
hot-wire igniter tip and hasten its demise. It is notable that the flashes of flame
(across the burner surface) sometimes continued briefly after the igniter was
deactivated and retracted. In one case on the first day of testing, there was excess
fuel and a ‘fireball’ was ignited which promptly quenched. Ignition also sometimes
failed due to a software limitation where the fuelFlowIgnitionDeltaMs parameter
which specifies the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation must be
evenly divisible by 100 (ms). This limitation wasn’t initially understood and the igniter
didn’t energize as a result.
From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere:
It was realized that the igniter for the burner gases could only be applied for up to
4 seconds, on insertion and retraction. This produced an unanticipated problem,
as the time for the burner gases to reach the igniter could be tens of seconds
depending on the flow rate. Also, after the first test, the burner would contain
that fuel mixture mixed with the chamber gas. Thus the burner would need to be
flushed with nitrogen before the second fuel mixture was initiated.
Intense communication with the NASA team proceeded the day before the first
test. The gas volume of the burner along with the feed pipe volume was supplied
by NASA. Accordingly ground experiments at UMD were conducted with an
identical NASA BRE burner along with its piping volume from the flow valve.
These experiments and theory were used to develop an algorithm for determining
the relative timing of the igniter and gas flow activation that will result in ignition.
Day 1 [of the first round] was conducted with rough estimates made on the fly,
and fortunately nearly all of the tests led to a satisfactory ignition. By Day 2 an
algorithm was established and successfully used for the remainder of the testing.
This algorithm will need to be refined and applied for the larger 50 mm diameter
burner that will be used in Round 2.
A document on the development of the algorithm and its refinement for the larger
burner [was] prepared and … shared with the NASA team to facilitate [ignition in]
round 2.
The second day of round-1 flame testing was delayed to allow for the development of
a new ignition procedure, where concerns arose that the mixture of gas flowing from
the burner wasn’t sufficiently well understood, i.e., in terms of concentrations. This
concern had to do with the burner’s large internal volume relative to that of the
burners used for the other ACME experiments. To be clear, this issue had to do with
the analysis of results rather than the achievement of ignition. Re-planning was also
necessary early in BRE testing because the test durations were often much longer than
had earlier been envisioned by the investigators. While these factors didn’t directly
interfere with the acquisition of test data, they did slow progress.
