ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
While it rarely occurred, BRE tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the
controlling software script), where that is typically prior to gas flow and the activation
of the igniter. As a result, there is little lost other than the time associated with the
failed test attempt. Such aborts typically occur because of communication issues with
an Image Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU).
ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel and nitrogen
have unfortunately not always performed adequately, where the flow rates have not
always been appropriately steady. The resulting effects on the flame behavior are
tentatively assumed to be minor, but this still needs to be assessed.
While it didn’t prevent the acquisition of scientific data, the intended igniter arm,
which establishes the relative positioning of the igniter tip and burner, was not found
for the round-2 hardware set-up. Therefore, an alternate arm, which positioned the
igniter further from the burner than intended, was used for the 3 Sept. 2020 testing.
Fortunately, the flames were still reliably ignited and the proper igniter arm was found
and installed prior to the subsequent test day.
However, it was determined that the 3 Sept. 2020 science objectives were not
accomplished because the fuel didn’t always transition to the intended test flow rate.
As a result of concerns about the ignition success because of the use of the alternate
igniter arm, the decision was made to repeatedly ignite the flame at the same fuel
flow rate and then subsequently adjust it to the desired test flow rate. The first
attempt was successful, but the transition time was shortened to save fuel, etc. which
unfortunately prevented the flow transition. In other words, the transition time was
too short where that wasn’t discovered until review of the data days later. As a result,
the tests were generally conducted at the same fuel flow rate, where that was meant
to be a variable. As a result, the data currently doesn’t allow a full assessment of the
effect of the burner size on the flammability. Therefore, a make-up test day in
Increment 64 has been planned to address this shortcoming.
During testing on 23 Dec. 2020, it was discovered that the lowest of the 14-micron
silicon carbide fibers on the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array had broken.
After some discussion, testing continued that day. Given that the translating array
had five ceramic fibers, the loss of one was not a significant science loss. But it was a
concern for crew safety. Recovery plans were developed and enacted on January 18
to remove the broken fragments from the harp-like array. Unfortunately, the next
fiber was broken during the delicate operations where the fibers are only spaced 5
mm apart. As a result, the last two BRE test days were conducted with only three
rather than five fibers in the TFP array. ACME does have alternate arrays, but also has
months of remaining testing, so the decision was made to continue testing with only
3 fibers.
115

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
C. Completeness/Quality of Data
The 194 flames ignited for BRE significantly exceeds the 73 tests which were specified as
required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD). As such, more
than 2.5 times as many flames were ignited than had been planned.
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not necessarily available for
all tests. Recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is done
because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed
per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some
image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted. This
is intentionally done to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the
project constraints.
From BRE Co-I Peter Sunderland:
The video and image data of the testing produced satisfactory data to display the
nature of the burning sequence from ignition to self-extinction or fuel termination.
However, the image quality is less than was hoped for. The ACME ops camera
provides video, but only offers 0.3 megapixels of resolution, and for many flames it is
too zoomed out. [As a clarification, the ops camera has a fixed lens and its primary
purpose is not flame measurements.] The GigE camera has poor sensitivity in the
blue, and after the ignition transient all our flames have been blue. This camera only
offers 1.4 megapixels of resolution and requires about 1 s exposures for blue flames,
which is far too slow to be considered video. The images provided by both cameras
are, according to UMD marketing staff, at too low resolution to be used in press
releases. In round 2 we will increase the gain on the GigE camera, an option we were
unaware of in round 1.
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware. But neglecting that
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually
become ‘hot’ over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing,
they are a degradation of the image quality.
See the discussion in III.D regarding fouling or degradation of the paint on the BRE
burner’s heat flux sensors.
It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there
is not obvious indication of such effects and it has thus far not been evaluated with
available measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS).
Note that although the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), in which the experiment is
conducted, is equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS) it was not utilized for
BRE (or any ACME) testing because of the crew time needed to enable and disable the
isolation before and after testing.
116

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
Regardless of the shortcomings discussed above, a great wealth of experimental data has
been secured and BRE’s first round is considered to be successful despite the frequent
saturation of the radiometer data discussed in section III.B.2. Meanwhile, the second
round is tentatively considered to be highly successful, where final assessment will
depend on further review and analysis of the data.
D. Status of Data Analysis (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral student
Parham Dehghani; lightly edited by Dennis Stocker)
All measured transient raw data (e.g., heat flux sensors, thermocouples, radiometers,
mass flow meters and chamber pressure sensor) have been converted to engineering
units and plotted using the calibrations provided in ACME’s Software Interface Design
Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D).
All of the round 1 and 2 tests have had the heat flux sensor data reduced using their
original calibrations. As presented below, the data is being processed to address the
effect of the combustion product water condensation on the sensor surfaces.
The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from
the flame to the burner surface. In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass
flow rate per unit area of the fuel mixture gives the heat of gasification of the emulated
fuel. The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of
gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in
an inert matrix). Thus, achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real
solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than for a candle flame, this
has not been shown before.
The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface.
One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center (r = 9.5 mm). As the sensors
are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the flame grows, water from its combustion
products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor. This occurs, as the dew point
for combustion products is about 60-70oC, and the sensor begins at ambient temperature
and can achieve temperatures over 100oC. Thus, condensation can occur at temperatures
below the dew point that lead to added heat to the sensor. Above the dew point, the
condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor. When the sensor is
dry and above 100oC, it will only measure the heat flux from the flame gases as intended.
We have duplicated this condensation effect in 1-g laboratory experiments with the
duplicative NASA BRE burner. Fig. 1 illustrates the condensation and evaporation effect
in the ISS tests. The offset sensor in red shows a clear jump increase when the water fully
evaporates. More analysis is needed to properly correct for this effect. Fortunately, by
the end of the test shown here (and for all of the other data), this water effect is gone.

E. Preliminary Research Findings (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral
student Parham Dehghani; lightly edited by Dennis Stocker)
The burner has shown that quasi-steady burning is possible for real solids with a flat
surface of 25 mm diameter. Up to now most flammability studies in microgravity have
focused on flame spread with a wind for concurrent spread and at least a self-induced
wind for opposed flow spread. We already knew that this would be possible from normal-
gravity research. The burning of liquids, as in a wick of a candle flame and small droplets,
has been shown to produce steady flames. However, many droplet flames were found to
extinguish owing to radiative cooling of the flame. We see this as well in the extended
ISS microgravity tests. However, this extinction was predominately seen for nominal
ambient conditions of 21% oxygen and 14.7 psia. At conditions of 27% oxygen, 10.2 psia
and 34% oxygen, 8.2 psia, the flames generally persisted for 3 minutes or more. These are
all atmospheric conditions that NASA is considering for future spacecraft
Figure 6 shows a typical test of ignition and flame growth. Although extinction occurred
at 45 s with the flame still growing, the heat flux was nearly steady by 30 s. Therefore, a
heat of gasification (L) could be estimated. This was done by using the arithmetic average
of the center and offset heat flux sensor as the net average heat flux.

The experimental flammability maps are shown in Figures 15 and 16. Both plots indicate
a decreasing, inverse asymptotic-like curve that approaches zero, for heat of gasification
with mass flux. It is surprising that the data cluster about a nearly singular trend.
However, both plots show that the heat of gasification is up to 20 % higher for the lower
heat of combustion 23.6 kJ/g. Our tests in the University of Maryland lab have shown,
with the BRE in 1-g that similar results for propane-nitrogen mixtures have the opposite
behavior with heats of gasification decreasing with heat of combustion for the same mass
flux. But again, the data mostly cluster about one trend line except for very low heats of
combustion. However, the corresponding 1-g heat of combustion data shift far to the
right and down from the microgravity data of Figures 15 and 16. For example, the 1-g
data would indicate ( 𝑚̇”,𝐿) points of about 30 g/m2s, 2 kJ/g and 10, 0.5. Moreover, our
previous work in a 5- s drop facility suggested similar data trends but with an apparent
vertical asymptote at about 3 g/m2s, rather than 1 as shown here. Obviously, the current
data at durations of minutes are more accurate than those limited to 5 s. However, it has
been shown that the ISS heat flux data even at self-extinction are theoretically nearly
steady. Figures 15 and 16 include the heats of gasification derived from the self-
extinguished endpoint data as well. Remarkably, the self-extinguished not-so-steady data
follow the same trend as the steady data.
Let us interpret Figures 15 and 16 in terms of the flammability of real materials in
microgravity. Typical melting plastics have heats of gasification ranging from about 2 to
3 kJ/g, with effective heats of gasification for charring plastics above 4 kJ/g. Some
selected literature values for materials with heats of combustion in the BRE range are
listed in Table 4. The accuracy of the calorimeter heat flux is found to be less than the
two sensors, thus, we relied on the arithmetic average of the two heat flux sensors data
for obtaining the flammability map. However, same results are shown considering the
calorimeter data. Figure 15 would suggest that polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP)
would burn in microgravity at about 3 g/m2s. Nylon and PMMA would burn at about 2.5
g/m2s, and the phenolic glass fiber composite would burn at about 1 g/m2s.

behavior with heats of gasification decreasing with heat of combustion for the same mass
flux. But again, the data mostly cluster about one trend line except for very low heats of
combustion. However, the corresponding 1-g heat of combustion data shift far to the
right and down from the microgravity data of Figures 15 and 16. For example, the 1-g
data would indicate ( 𝑚̇”,𝐿) points of about 30 g/m2s, 2 kJ/g and 10, 0.5. Moreover, our
previous work in a 5- s drop facility suggested similar data trends but with an apparent
vertical asymptote at about 3 g/m2s, rather than 1 as shown here. Obviously, the current
data at durations of minutes are more accurate than those limited to 5 s. However, it has
been shown that the ISS heat flux data even at self-extinction are theoretically nearly
steady. Figures 15 and 16 include the heats of gasification derived from the self-
extinguished endpoint data as well. Remarkably, the self-extinguished not-so-steady data
follow the same trend as the steady data.
Let us interpret Figures 15 and 16 in terms of the flammability of real materials in
microgravity. Typical melting plastics have heats of gasification ranging from about 2 to
3 kJ/g, with effective heats of gasification for charring plastics above 4 kJ/g. Some
selected literature values for materials with heats of combustion in the BRE range are
listed in Table 4. The accuracy of the calorimeter heat flux is found to be less than the
two sensors, thus, we relied on the arithmetic average of the two heat flux sensors data
for obtaining the flammability map. However, same results are shown considering the
calorimeter data. Figure 15 would suggest that polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP)
would burn in microgravity at about 3 g/m2s. Nylon and PMMA would burn at about 2.5
g/m2s, and the phenolic glass fiber composite would burn at about 1 g/m2s.

Round 2 tests were finished with 196 successful ignitions. The measured heat flux by the
transducers were used and the end point data of the long-duration tests (i.e., the tests in
which the fuel flow was terminated as opposed to the tests that self-extinguished) were
used to obtain heats of gasification. The heats of gasification of these data from round 2
testing as a function of fuel mixture mass flux are shown in Fig. 19. One important fire

safety consideration, based on the findings of this study, is that solid materials with heats
of combustion in the range 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification from about 1 to 10
kJ/g can burn in microgravity. The NASA alternative flammability Test 2 [1] using the Cone
Calorimeter can measure these material properties. As this study develops a more
complete understanding, NASA may wish to put more emphasis into Test 2.
Moreover, the flammability map based on our theoretical analysis is shown in Figure 17.
It shows similar asymptotic trend and clearly indicates lower pressure and higher oxygen
concentration as favorable conditions for long duration burning.

The imaging data from ops camera and ACME camera are used to create videos and image
sequences for all of the tests. Preliminary analysis on the first three days of the second
round of ISS testing data was performed. Pure methane was the fuel used for testing on

was hard to ignite compared to ethylene and flames tend to self-extinguish faster even at
a high oxygen concentration.
A new method is used to examine the asymptotic behavior of the heat flux data. The
inverse of the burn-time was used as the abscissa and the transient data from the two
heat flux sensors are shown in Figure 18 for one of the tests.

Appendix G. Astronauts and Cosmonauts who Conducted ISS
Operations for BRE
This list was prepared by Dennis Stocker from his log of ACME operations.
Ten cosmonauts and astronauts participated in ISS operations directly supporting the BRE investigation,
where they are listed with the dates of their activity (at least as planned). They are listed by the number
of days in which they conducted supporting on-orbit activities and alphabetically. The crew activity on
each of those dates is very briefly summarized in the Appendix F. Additional information about the crew
activity can be found in some of the subsequent appendices.
The CIR and ACME hardware was initially set up for BRE testing by Canadian astronaut David Saint-Jacques,
while U.S. astronaut Chris Cassidy reconfigured the hardware for BRE’s second round of testing after
intervening testing for other experiments. Meanwhile, the gas bottles were most often replaced by
Russian cosmonauts Oleg Kononenko and Sergey Kud-Sverchkov.

Appendix H. ISS Operations per the Payload Weekly Science Summary
This section is from Dennis Stocker’s log of ACME operations.
BRE round 1, featuring tests with ethylene and the 25-mm burner
2019
Week 16: January 11-17
David: On GMT 014, thank you for replacing the imaging modules in the CIR LLL-UV Imaging Package. Then
on GMT 018, great job configuring the back of the CIR Optics Bench to support future ACME experiments.
We appreciate all your hard work and diligence during the many intricate tasks!
Week 18: January 25-31
David: On GMT 031 & 032, great job configuring the ACME Chamber Insert to support the next ACME
experiment, BRE (Burning Rate Emulator). We appreciate your attention to detail during the many
complicated tasks! We especially appreciate you taking all the closeout photos of the newly installed
hardware. We will check out and calibrate the newly installed hardware next week and perform the first
test points late next week.
Week 19: February 1-7
Oleg & Anne: Great job replacing the CIR Manifold & GC Bottles this week! We these new bottles installed,
we look forward to starting the next ACME experiment, BRE (Burning Rate Emulator).
Week 20: February 8-14
On GMT 039, we performed our first ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points. Unlike the other
ACME experiments, BRE is focused on improving spacecraft fire safety rather than practical terrestrial
combustion. More specifically, BRE uses gaseous fuels to determine the flammability of liquids and solids
in microgravity by selecting test conditions to match key parameters. We performed nine successful tests
burning ethylene on the 25-mm diameter burner, where the burner’s embedded sensors measure the
heat flux that would normally vaporize a liquid or solid fuel. The tests were conducted under a range of
oxygen concentrations and pressures, including some atmospheres that could be used for future crew
vehicles or habitats.

Figure 1 shows a sequence of three images from BRE’s first on-orbit test. The first image shows that the
flame grew to become nominally hemispherical (over the burner outlet, which can also be seen). The
second image shows a hole in the top of the flame due to radiative heat loss. However, the third image

shows that the flame recovered, where the hole closed. In this latter phase of the test, measurements of
chemiluminescence (from OH*) clearly reveal that the flame was oscillating at approximately 1 Hz. These
oscillations (the opening and closing of the flame’s top) were seen to grow in magnitude and are
associated with the flame’s approach to extinction. In the first test, this lasted for an extended time, but
in other tests at lower oxygen concentrations the oscillations sometimes lasted 10 seconds or less before
the flame quenched. BRE seeks to understand the flame extinction and the conditions under which the
flames become unsteady and finally extinguish.
Week 21: February 15-21
Testing for the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment resumed on GMT 051 following a revision of the
ignition procedure. Eight successful tests were conducted burning pure ethylene, which is naturally a
sooty fuel because of its double bond, but the soot produced during ignition quickly vanished leaving a
pale blue flame, where the flame temperatures were insufficient to generate soot. These flames grow to
be nominally hemispherical, then become quasi-steady although weakening, and finally become unsteady
and extinguish when radiative heat losses become too great. The experiment’s goal is to improve our
understanding of material flammability in microgravity and thereby guide the selection of materials use
in spacecraft.
CAPTION TO VIDEO, WHICH IS NOT INCLUDED IN THIS LOG
The video from test 19039G1 is typical of the BRE tests conducted thus far, where the flame grows
to become nominally hemispherical, during which time the soot produced at ignition vanishes.
The flame then becomes quasi-steady, e.g., in terms of the flame shape and size, although it can
be seen that the flame weakens with time – becoming dimmer and more diffuse. Oxygen
transport to the flame is inhibited because it is blanketed by an ever-thickening cloud of carbon
dioxide and water vapor. Eventually, radiative heat loss leads the top of the flame (on the video’s
left) to locally extinguish, leaving a hole in the flame. But the fuel and oxygen, which are normally
separated by the flame, mix and the flame quickly reestablishes, filling the hole. A pattern of
oscillation begins, which also features periodic lifting of the flame base from the cylindrical burner
(on the right of the video). The oscillations grow in strength, where the flame becomes
momentarily just a ring. At the end, before complete extinction, the flame also partially detaches
from the burner, leaving a crack in the flame’s side extending from the base to its top.
The durations of at least the quasi-steady and unsteady periods are strongly dependent on the
atmosphere in the chamber, where both the oxygen concentration and pressure have been
varied. As one might expect, longer durations are observed at higher oxygen concentrations.
Note that the brighter circle that can be seen in upper middle of the video is due to reflection from
an optical sensor, which is not seen in the other three camera views.
Week 22: February 22-28
On GMT 056, we performed ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points with a 50% ethylene/50%
nitrogen mixture. The flames with 50% ethylene may be steadier than the 100% ethylene flames, which
require more oxygen at the same total flow rate. The 50% ethylene flames still exhibited flame growth, a
quasi-steady period, and oscillations leading to extinction. The flames also quickly became soot free (i.e.,
all blue flame) after ignition.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
Ignition, extinction, and the three main phases of the BRE flame’s life can be seen in this example plot of
the OH* chemiluminescence measured by one of the three PhotoMultipiler Tube (PMT) modules on the
ACME Chamber Insert. OH* is an excited molecule that loses energy by emitting a photon of light at a
specific wavelength (in the ultraviolet). In combustion of most fuels, there is oxygen, hydrogen, and lots
of energy making OH* measurements a good indicator of the flame.
This data shows that the flame is weakening during the quasi-steady period when the flame size and shape
is nominally constant. The OH* measurement also clearly shows the oscillations that precede extinction
and their growing strength. The flame’s oscillations (e.g., with the opening and closing of the top) are at
a nominally constant frequency that is a little less than 1 Hz. The huge OH* oscillations are the flame’s
death throes when it splits open from bottom to top and partially detaches from the burner.
Week 23: March 1-7
On GMT 064, Oleg Kononenko replaced the CIR Manifold #2 Bottle that was consumed during test points
on GMT 063. For these ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points, we used higher fuel flow rates with
the same fuel (50% ethylene/50% nitrogen) as the test points on GMT 056. We performed a total of six
tests, where the first—in an atmosphere of 40% oxygen—was notable in that the flame didn’t extinguish
during the five-minute test even though it was oscillating in the last three minutes. As expected, the flames
in subsequent tests with higher flow rates grew to be significantly larger in size, and with their higher
oxygen consumption, they extinguished in significantly shorter times. We observed dramatic oscillations
with the large flames. Furthermore, these large oscillating flames became asymmetric; whereas, smaller
BRE flames have been largely axisymmetric even when oscillating.

and a highly dynamic spiral extending upward. As in previous tests, the flame partially detaches
from the burner (right side of video), but in this case, the flame surprisingly persists for roughly

Week 24/01: March 8-14
On GMT 072, Oleg Kononenko replaced the CIR Manifold #4 Bottle to support upcoming ACME BRE test
points with pure ethylene fuel, and he installed the CIR Manifold #1 Bottle to support the upcoming CIR
FOMA Calibration.
On GMT 066 & 070, we performed the remaining ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points using
diluted ethylene fuel (50% ethylene/50% nitrogen). These tests were conducted with low fuel flow rates
under atmospheric conditions that could be used for future crew exploration vehicles (or habitats), i.e.,
with elevated oxygen concentrations (between 26% and 36%) and reduced pressures. Compared to prior
tests, these flames were steady and didn’t extinguish during the allotted test durations.
Even though these flames appeared steady, measurements of OH* and CH* chemiluminescence revealed
that they were slowly weakening as each test progressed. Chemiluminescence occurs when excited
molecules at a high energy state drop to a lower energy state by emitting a photon of a certain
wavelength. CH* chemiluminescence is why hydrocarbon flames are blue; meanwhile the OH*
chemiluminescence is in the ultraviolet.
Although the flames were weakening, the thermal radiation from each flame slowly increased because of
the lack of buoyancy, which, in gravity, removes the hot combustion gases from the vicinity of a flame.
Instead, these flames became blanketed by a thickening cloud of hot and radiating combustion products,
namely carbon dioxide and water vapor. This accumulation of products inhibited the transport of oxygen
to the flame. Yet, with the low flow of diluted fuel, the oxygen diffusion was enough to maintain these
flames during each test’s duration. If the test durations weren’t limited, these flames would have
eventually gone out, but it could have taken many minutes for that to happen.

Week 22: September 4-10
On GMT 247, we began the second round of testing for ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) with 13 flames
ignited using ethylene fuel. While the first round of testing only used the 25-mm diameter burner, this
round of testing began with the 50-mm diameter burner to better understand the effect of burner size on
flame behavior. Even though these flames burned for a long time, they were unsteady and extremely
dynamic. Since BRE’s research focus is on quasi-steady flame behavior, the remaining tests will use the
25-mm burner.
In many of these 50-mm burner tests, heat loss caused the top of the flame to locally quench—creating a
hole that allowed for increased mixing of the fuel and oxygen. The flame was able to reestablish, closing
the hole in its top. These oscillations occurred repeatedly and grew in strength such that the flame became
a ring instead of a dome. Later in the burn, the flame often partially detached from the burner, creating a
hole in the side of the flame that would also open and close repeatedly. In some cases, this behavior
transitioned to a more constant hole, where the partial flame would swirl around the burner’s rim as if it
were “chasing its tail.”

ACME BRE Test Point Image
This preliminary false-colored image of a dome-shaped flame shows an array of 14-micron ceramic fibers
making temperature measurements. The four visible fibers pass through or near the flame and glow
because of the high temperature. This flame, which is non-premixed, is like a bubble in that the methane
fuel is inside the bubble and the oxygen is outside the bubble. The flame shell, like the film of a bubble, is
a thin sheet where the methane and oxygen come together and react, producing carbon dioxide, water
vapor, light, and heat. The fibers are only visible where they are hot, near the flame shell, which is why
the centers of the three lower fibers are not visible.
The temperature profile along each fiber is optically determined from its varying hue through a technique
known as Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP). In this image, the blue has been enhanced so that the soot-free
flame is clearly visible along with the much brighter fibers, which naturally transition from red to orange
to yellow as the temperature increases.

Upon ignition, the ethylene flame in this video clip exhibits a lot of soot, which is bright whitish-
yellow in appearance. On Earth, soot is normally consumed as it passes through the flame sheet,
but in this test point the soot particles are large enough to escape the flame. In microgravity, soot

temperatures are required to create the soot and microgravity conditions can lead to lower flame
temperatures. There is no buoyancy to bring in fresh oxygen and the combustion products blanket
these low-momentum flames. The carbon dioxide, water vapor, and soot contribute to radiative
heat loss. This video clip ends as the flame becomes mostly blue and soot-free.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022
ACME BRE Graph
This graph shows as a function of time, the fuel flow (red) and three optical flame measurements from a
test in which pure ethylene was burned. The optical flame measurements were made with
Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules of OH* chemiluminescence (purple), CH* chemiluminescence (light
blue), and broadband emissions in the visible and near UV spectrum (dark blue). OH* and CH* are
transient molecules which, in the process of chemiluminescence, emit a photon at specific wavelengths
when they drop to a lower energy level. The CH* chemiluminescence is the principal source of the blue
seen in hydrocarbon flames, while OH* is in the ultraviolet and is used in ACME to indicate ignition and
extinction.
The initially sooty flame was ignited at 32 seconds, after which the hot-wire igniter was retracted. At about
60 seconds, after the ceramic fiber array was inserted, the flame became quasi-steady. But the PMT
signals weakened with time, where the low-momentum flame became increasingly blanketed by carbon
dioxide and water vapor in the absence of buoyancy.
At about 95 seconds, the increasing radiative loss caused the flame’s top to quench, creating a hole in the
flame. This hole allowed the fuel and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame, to directly mix.
This mixing enhanced flammability, and the flame quickly reestablished and closed the hole, but then
again, it locally quenched. This oscillatory behavior happened repeatedly at roughly 1 Hz with the flame
opening growing with time until the flame became just a ring. We saw this phenomenon in the first round
of BRE testing performed on ISS in 2019. A paper about computational modeling of it is now in press.
At about 135 seconds, the flame began to partially detach from the rim of the burner and then reattach
until it completely extinguished at 148 seconds.

and made available via e-mail or online via www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/.
Note that hyperlinks were generally not included in the excerpts below, but they typically go to web pages
accessible via https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/experiments/explorer/. Those

Week of January 28, 2019
Other work was performed on these investigations: …
• The Advanced Combustion Microgravity Experiment (ACME) investigation is a set of five
independent studies of gaseous flames to be conducted in the Combustion Integration Rack (CIR).
Week of February 4, 2019
Other work was performed on these investigations and facilities:
• CIR includes an optics bench, combustion chamber, fuel and oxidizer control, and five different
cameras for performing combustion experiments in microgravity.
Week of February 25, 2019
Studying gaseous flames and flammability
Following replacement of an ACME fuel flow controller, which allows observation of different flow
conditions, the crew documented its final configuration with photographs. The ACME series performed in
the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) includes five independent studies of gaseous flames. The current
experiment, Burning Rate Emulator (BRE), focuses on spacecraft fire prevention, specifically improving
understanding of materials flammability and assessing existing flammability test methods in low and
partial-gravity environments.

Week of August 31, 2020
Space Station Science Image of the Week: CIR
NASA astronaut Chris Cassidy changed out the experiments in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) this
past week. These investigations could help us learn about fire prevention in space.
Week of September 28, 2020
Testing fire safety in space
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) fire safety study aims at improving our fundamental understanding of
the flammability of certain materials and assesses whether existing flammability test methods are
appropriate for low and partial-gravity environments. BRE is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack
(CIR) as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. The crew
exchanged a gas chromatograph bottle for conducting the second part of BRE.
This image shows a dome-shaped flame and the burner illuminated in red on the left during a BRE test in
an atmosphere of about 30% oxygen. Future crew exploration missions may feature vehicles and habitats
at elevated oxygen concentrations, and these conditions present increased fire hazard.
Credits: NASA

The subsequent text was prepared by Dennis Stocker, where the source information is available from
https://blogs.nasa.gov/stationreport. Text was added identifying the investigation’s two rounds, but BRE
operations listed under the headings “All activities are complete unless otherwise noted” or “Completed
Task List Activities” were not included in this report. Some days of crew activity were only listed in those
ways and as a result this section does not comprehensively document crew activity in support of the BRE
experiment.

2019 January 14: GMT 014
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) imaging reconfiguration: Today the crew replaced a filter module and
relay optics module. This is part of the reconfiguration to support the upcoming Burning Rate Emulator
(BRE) series of experiments. These reconfiguration activities are expected to continue over the next two
to three weeks. The BRE experiment runs are focused on spacecraft fire prevention. More specifically,
BRE’s objective is to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability and to assess the
relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.
2019 January 18: GMT 018
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) Hardware Reconfiguration: As a continuation of the ongoing CIR
reconfiguration for the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) BRE (Burning Rate
Emulator) investigation, the crew replaced the relay optics module in the CIR HiBMS (High Bit depth Multi
Spectral) Imaging Package, installed the CIR LLL-UV (Low Light Level Ultraviolet) Imaging Package, and
installed the FCF IPSU (Fluids and Combustion Facility Image Processing and Storage Unit). The BRE
experiment is focused on spacecraft fire prevention. More specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve our
fundamental understanding of materials flammability and to assess the relevance of existing flammability
test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.
2019 January 31: GMT 031
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME): A crewmember replaced hardware on the
ACME unit by installing a new mesh power supply and closeout panel. The ACME experiment series being
performed in the CIR includes five independent studies of gaseous flames. The primary goals of ACME are
to improve fuel efficiency and reduce pollutant production in routine fuel combustion activities on Earth.
Its secondary goal is to improve spacecraft fire prevention through innovative research focused on
materials flammability.
2019 February 1: GMT 032

record portions of the CIR ACME reconfiguration and chamber insertion into the CIR rack. ISS Experience
creates a virtual reality film documenting daily life aboard the space station. The 8 to 10 minute videos
created from footage taken during the six-month investigation cover different aspects of crew life,
execution of science aboard the station, and the international partnerships involved. The ISS Experience
uses a Z-CAM V1 Pro Cinematic VR (Virtual Reality) 360-degree camera with nine 190° fisheye lenses.

ACME hardware reconfiguration. The ACME experiment series being performed in the CIR includes five

2020 September 14: GMT 258
Burning Rate Emulator (BRE): The crew reconfigured the ACME hardware in preparation for BRE
experiment runs. This includes swapping in Igniter Arm #2. The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) investigation
is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS), as part of
the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. In this fire safety study, the
flammability of solid and liquid materials is simulated by burning gaseous fuels under key conditions
corresponding to the solid and liquid materials. This technique has been demonstrated for a wide variety
of materials in normal-gravity and could provide an efficient way to screen and select fire-resistant
materials for use in spacecraft, if the technique is similarly effective in microgravity.
2020 September 22: GMT 266
Combustion Integrated Rack/Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (CIR/ACME)/BRE-
2: The crew exchanged a 40% oxygen/60% nitrogen bottle at the manifold 2 location for a new bottle with
the same composition. They also replaced the ethylene manifold 4 bottle with a methane bottle, but
were not able to open the bottle valve. CIR powered ops for today have been cancelled while the ground
team discusses the issue. This was performed in support of the continuing BRE part 2 (Burning Rate
Emulator) investigation, which is one of the ACME suite of five gas combustion experiments. The BRE
experiment runs are focused on spacecraft fire prevention. More specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve
our fundamental understanding of materials flammability and to assess the relevance of existing
flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.

Appendix N. Summary of the ISS data collection
The BRE data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other
ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were
subsequently transported to the ground.
The BRE image data includes images from the following cameras:
1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but
those settings were consistent within each individual test)
2. CFI intensified camera, typically used with a CH* filter (and likely always or nearly always for BRE)
3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the
opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off
The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, and
HiBMs cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video was
recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format.
The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software
Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D).
The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through
NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

O.3 Awards
University of Maryland graduate student Michael Bustamante was selected as a NASA Space
Technology Research Fellow for 2011/2012 for work on the BRE project, a distinct honor described at
https://fpe.umd.edu/release/fire-protection-experts-available-to-the-media.
For his work on BRE, Akshit Markan was awarded the University of Maryland Graduate School’s
Outstanding Graduate Assistant Award for 2017. Markan’s recognition for his outstanding work is
further described at https://fpe.umd.edu/news/story/fpe-phd-candidate-wins-2017-outstanding-
graduate-assistant-award. It explains, for example, that only the top 2% of Graduate Assistants were
selected for this honor.
In 2021, BRE Co-Investigator Peter Sunderland was inducted as a Fellow in the Combustion Institute
for his “significant contributions to understanding laminar flame dynamics and soot formation and
oxidation.”
O.4 Outreach
NASA Project Scientists Dennis Stocker created the Space Flames Facebook page
(www.facebook.com/space.flames) and Flickr site (https://www.flickr.com/photos/space-flames),
where some entries are specific to BRE. He continues to administer these sites, where most content
has been about the ACME project of which BRE is a part. Meanwhile, Stocker has made educational
and general information is available via https://tinyurl.com/space-flames. As an educational example,
a simple board game related to the ACME’s spherical flames experiments, which can be downloaded.
As another example, an ACME information sheet providing an overview and recent status can also be
downloaded through that site. Such flyers have been distributed at meetings of The Combustion
Institute and the American Society for Gravitational and Space Research (ASGSR). Other documents,
including the BRE Science Requirements Document (SRD), are available for download from
https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/space/iss-research/iss-fcf/cir/acme/downloads/.
The University of Maryland promoted awareness of the BRE investigation online, where that has
included precursor ground-based research as well as the ISS testing, as can be seen via these links:

Meanwhile, NASA promoted awareness of ISS combustion research with the video ‘The Power of
Studying Combustion on the ISS’ which was posted on March 13, 2018.
Awareness of ISS combustion research, including the ACME project, was promoted on Oct. 15, 2018
by The Combustion Institute in their online news article, “International Space Station (ISS) Combustion
Experiments.”
Stocker is involved in a broad range of NASA educational outreach to students and teachers, Scouts
of both genders, and the general public. His primary outreach focus is the fundamentals of
microgravity (for which resources are available via http://tinyurl.com/SEECmicrogravity) and human
spaceflight. But he periodically addresses other topics, e.g., where he sometimes speaks on ‘NASA
and the Science of Superman’ – for example at the Superman Celebration in Metropolis, IL. In this
regard, his NASA outreach is carried out locally, regionally, nationally, and online. For example, he
regularly presents on microgravity at Space Center Houston’s Space Exploration Educators Conference
(SEEC). He has exhibited the last five National Scout Jamborees, four national Boy Scout conferences,
the last three national Girl Scout conventions, and the 2019 World Scout Jamboree (which was held
in the U.S.). Stocker has been a key lead for the agency in NASA’s participation in these Scouting
events, where as an example the latter outreach is visually described at
www.nasa.gov/feature/stem/world-scout-jamboree.html.
